topics.title: 27.1.1 Choosing Indicators and Denominators
topics.summary: A service-level indicator must specify which events count as good and which events enter the denominator. For a submission API, a good event might mean a valid new request is durably accepted within a latency threshold. For the job service as a whole, it might mean an accepted job completes within a business deadline. These are different indicators.

topics.title: 27.1.2 Interpreting Error Budgets Without False Precision
topics.summary: An error budget is the allowed bad-event fraction under the selected objective and window. For a request-count objective of 99.9 percent over 10,000 eligible requests, the allowance is ten bad requests. If seven are bad, 70 percent of that allowance is consumed under this simplified model.

topics.summary: Measure arrival rate, service time, backlog age, storage growth, and resource utilization under representative work. A job count without input cost can mislead capacity planning. topics.title: 27.3.1 Defining Recovery Point and Recovery Time
topics.summary: Recovery point describes how much state loss is acceptable under a stated failure scenario. Recovery time describes how long restoration of the required service can take. A backup interval alone does not establish either value; restore procedures, dependencies, and reconciliation affect them.

topics.title: 27.3.2 Closing an Incident with a Causal Review
topics.summary: A postmortem should distinguish trigger, contributing conditions, impact, detection, mitigation, and prevention. “The database was slow” may describe a symptom without explaining why new work was admitted without a bound or why every client retried simultaneously.

cards.question: Explain Closing an Incident with a Causal Review in your own words.

blocks.text: Use a timeline with event meanings and clock limitations. Correlate deployment changes, error categories, queue growth, and state transitions. Avoid declaring causality merely because two graphs changed at similar wall times.

blocks.text: Corrective actions should address mechanisms and have verification criteria. “Be more careful” is weak. “Reject new work when durable pending count reaches the configured limit, and add a test that preserves duplicate lookup while full” is concrete and testable.

blocks.text: Recovery ends when the relevant service contract is restored, not merely when the process is alive. Verify backlog clearance, status accuracy, resumed admission, and the absence of unresolved ambiguous effects. Document remaining risk and assign ownership for follow-up work.

reading.title: 27.3.2 Closing an Incident with a Causal Review
paragraphs: A postmortem should distinguish trigger, contributing conditions, impact, detection, mitigation, and prevention. “The database was slow” may describe a symptom without explaining why new work was admitted without a bound or why every client retried simultaneously.

Use a timeline with event meanings and clock limitations. Correlate deployment changes, error categories, queue growth, and state transitions. Avoid declaring causality merely because two graphs changed at similar wall times.

Corrective actions should address mechanisms and have verification criteria. “Be more careful” is weak. “Reject new work when durable pending count reaches the configured limit, and add a test that preserves duplicate lookup while full” is concrete and testable.

Recovery ends when the relevant service contract is restored, not merely when the process is alive. Verify backlog clearance, status accuracy, resumed admission, and the absence of unresolved ambiguous effects. Document remaining risk and assign ownership for follow-up work.

reading.title: Engineering case — Close an incident only after the backlog is reconciled
paragraphs: At 09:00 the worker becomes unavailable. The gateway accepts jobs until its pending limit is reached, then returns BUSY for new keys. At 09:10 the worker restarts and answers health probes. Declaring full recovery at 09:10 ignores the accepted backlog and the clients still waiting for results.

Track at least three phases: dependency reachability restored, backlog processing resumed, and the relevant completion objective recovered. Their timestamps can differ substantially. A large replay surge can also cause a second slowdown, so restoration should remain subject to capacity and retry controls.

The incident report should distinguish rejected new work from accepted delayed work. Rejected callers need an explicit retry or resubmission policy. Accepted callers should retain their existing keys and query status. Mixing those groups can produce either lost intent or unnecessary duplicate logical jobs.

After processing resumes, reconcile gateway completion and worker receipts for a bounded relevant set. An unresolved mismatch may indicate a lost response, a permanent conflict, or a damaged state file. Do not clear pending rows merely to make the dashboard green; each row represents an obligation that needs a terminal outcome or authorized repair.

The postmortem can identify a trigger, such as a worker deployment, and contributing conditions, such as insufficient capacity margin or unclear readiness. Corrective actions should be verifiable: a deployment check for schema compatibility, an alert on pending age, or a test that preserves duplicate lookup while the queue is full.

Avoid using one availability percentage to summarize every consequence. A ten-minute outage affecting only status reads differs from ten minutes of lost accepted jobs. The metric definition should preserve the outcome that matters to the service’s users.
